title: Lenten customs
hookLine: Friday fish, Stations, and a box for the poor

lines: A BOX ON THE KITCHEN COUNTER.
cards: A Friday in March. The church hall smells of fried fish, and a volunteer in an apron is handing out paper plates of cod and coleslaw.
Upstairs, at seven, a small group walks slowly around the church, stopping at each of the stations on the walls.
At home, on the kitchen counter, sits a little cardboard box with a slot in the top, and the coins rattle when someone moves it to wipe the counter. None of this happens at Mass.
It happens in halls, hallways and kitchens, where Lent lives as much as in church.

teach.b: You met these three in your first year: prayer, fasting and almsgiving. In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus says to do all three quietly.
On alms, the Douay-Rheims has him say: "But when thou dost alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth." Each custom fits under one of them. Friday fish belongs to fasting.
Church law makes Fridays days of penance and names abstinence from meat as a Friday practice, kept with special care in Lent.

Fish isn't counted as meat, so it often lands on the Friday table, and some parishes hold fish fries. The point isn't the fish. It's the meat you went without, and the reminder that Friday is the day of the cross.
The Stations of the Cross belong to prayer. On Lenten Fridays, some parishes walk the stations together, stopping at each image of Jesus's last journey, from his condemnation to the tomb.
It's a prayer you do with your feet.

teach.h: A BOX FOR THE POOR, FOR ALMS.
teach.b: The box for the poor belongs to almsgiving. Families keep a small box or jar through Lent, drop in what they saved by skipping a treat or eating simply, and bring it to church at the end.

That's the quiet logic of Lent: the three feed each other. What you give up in fasting, you give away in alms, and you carry both into prayer. It works best in a kitchen, on an ordinary weekday, with nobody watching.

teach.h: LET NOT THY LEFT HAND KNOW.

how: In Lent, Catholics abstain from meat on Fridays, and some parishes hold fish fries and pray the Stations of the Cross on Friday evenings. Some families keep a box or jar for alms at home and give what they save to the poor at the end of Lent.

s: the point of Friday fish is the fish
the point is going without meat on the day of the cross; fish just isn't counted as meat.
the Lenten practices can feed each other
what's saved by fasting can become alms, and both are carried into prayer.
Jesus tells his followers to give alms where everyone can see
he says the opposite: "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth."

games.q: it's a Lenten Friday. you skipped the steak and saved some money. what does the logic of Lent suggest you do with the savings?
o: drop it in the box for the poor.
nothing; going without was the whole point.
games.why: fasting, almsgiving and prayer belong together: what you give up in the fast, you give away in alms.

practice: Look at the three: going without something, like meat on a Friday; walking and praying, like the Stations; setting money aside for someone in need, like the box on the counter.

Pick the one you could actually do this week at home, and see exactly where it would happen: which meal, which corner, which jar. If you pray, offer it to God; if you don't, decide quietly and tell no one.

wordCard.voice: Lenten customs. Friday fish, the Stations of the Cross, and a box for the poor: fasting, prayer and almsgiving, kept at home and in the parish. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the Way of the Cross: the Church's name for the Stations.

carryVoice: Your line: lent at home. Fasting, prayer and alms, in a kitchen as much as a church. Until tomorrow.
